newsitem.title: ITALY: Olivetti board meets after share drops.
newsitem.headline: Olivetti board meets after share drops.

text.p: The board of troubled information and technology group Olivetti held a meeting in Milan on Tuesday after the group's shares dropped five percent amid persistent rumours of conflict amid top management at the company.

Olivetti shares slumped seven percent on the bourse, close to a record low of 681 lire (45 cents) in July this year, before closing five percent down at 726 lire per share as speculation also mounted over the state of the company's financial health.
Sources close to the company said the meeting, held in Milan not at the group's north western Ivrea headquarters, "could be long" but they gave no details of the agenda.
Olivetti itself made no comment on the rumours, which sent the share price tumbling for the second day in a row.
"What the small investor is seeing is a kind of Titanic and everyone is trying to bail out," said Alberto Rolla, analyst at brokers Pasfin in Milan.

Analysts and traders said concern centred on talk of conflict between Olivetti chairman Carlo De Benedetti and new managing director Francesco Caio, who took over in July, and on the possibility of larger than expected losses.
Caio, former head of Olivetti's 41.3 percent owned cellular phone company Omnitel, replaced Corrado Passera who resigned suddenly.
Newspapers reported rumours of renewed losses of 300 billion lire ($198 million) for the first half of 1996.

"I've heard the rumour of a 300 billion loss for the first half which would be a staggering number. That's the worry -- that there's another nasty surprise in terms of earnings, or lack of them," said an analyst at a UK securities house who asked not to be named.
Many analysts expect Olivetti to make a loss in 1996, although the company said early this year it hoped to return to the black this year.
Il Sole 24 Ore financial daily cited the possibility the group would make provisions for further restructuring charges, which would weigh on the balance sheet.
Olivetti launched a 2.257 trillion lire rights issue nearly year ago to restructure and then announced at the start of 1996 its restructuring charge would be higher than first expected.
Il Sole speculated the company would exit the highly competitive personal computer sector once and for all, leaving further losses on its balance sheet.

The stock, which has been on a steady overall decline since April 1994, took a steeper turn for the worse last week in the wake of news foreign institutional investors with a 25 percent shareholding met to force the company to boost its share value.
"It's all rumour driven, but you know in Italy the market is never completely wrong," one trader here said.
Olivetti has not broken even since 1990 and made a record loss of 1.589 trillion lire ($1.05 billion) in 1995.

It is due to report first half 1996 results on September 26 but said back in July its PC company, widely regarded as the biggest thorn in its side, made a pretax profit in the second quarter after a loss in the first.
Analysts say the lack of comment from Olivetti has been part of the stock's problem, with several saying they had called the group for clarification and got no response.
"They are not talking," Rolla said. "The fact that they are leaving the market without any information means that the market is wondering what is really happening."
